name: Cyber
baseline: Lua (PUC-Rio), LuaJIT and QuickJS (also Janet on the fiber test)
workload: Recursive Fibonacci, range/iterator loops and a fiber (coroutine) benchmark in VM mode and JIT mode, from the project's performance page.
claimed_speedup: Per a search snippet of cyberscript.dev/performance.html: fib (VM) Cyber 19 ms vs LuaJIT 21 ms vs Lua 39 ms (about 2x faster than Lua, derived from page data); fiber benchmark 8.01x faster than Lua, 2.77x faster than LuaJIT, 6.28x faster than Janet; range/iterator (VM) LuaJIT 11 ms, Cyber 12 ms, Lua 27 ms, QuickJS 78 ms (Cyber slightly slower than LuaJIT, faster than Lua and QuickJS); fib (JIT) Cyber and LuaJIT both 5 ms.
tradeoffs: Written in Zig and built with the Zig toolchain; embeddable through a C API (libcyber, see examples/libcyber in the repo), so usable from C++ via C, but the language itself is new, dynamically typed and not Lua-compatible. A stencil-based JIT was still being written in December 2025 (x64 stencils, refactored JIT backend) and the language has been reworked repeatedly, so benchmark numbers may not match current master.
caveats: Snippet only: the numbers come from a WebSearch snippet of cyberscript.dev/performance.html, which is blocked here (EGRESS_BLOCKED when opened); hardware, compiler flags and Lua/LuaJIT/QuickJS versions were not seen. The repo's examples/README links the benchmark code at test/bench, but master has no test directory (404), so the comparison could not be reproduced or inspected. First-party numbers; the snippet itself says the JIT is recent and has few benchmarks.
found_via: WebSearch 'Cyber scripting language performance benchmark vs Lua LuaJIT QuickJS fubark' (cyberscript.dev/performance.html snippet), first surfaced by 'fast embeddable scripting language benchmark faster than Lua QuickJS engineering blog'

name: Apogee (Lua 5.5 VM in Go, formerly luart)
baseline: C Lua 5.5 (PUC-Rio; Lua 5.4.9 on the Apple M1 run) and Shopify/go-lua
workload: 17 standard benchmarks (14 Are We Fast Yet ports plus binary-trees, fannkuch-redux and spectral-norm from the Benchmarks Game) and an 11-workload embedding suite; geometric mean of per-benchmark time divided by C Lua's time.
claimed_speedup: With the JIT, 0.57x of C Lua 5.5's time (about 1.75x faster, derived from page data) on a Ryzen 9 9900X3D, faster than C Lua on all 17 standard benchmarks (Mandelbrot 0.20x, spectral-norm 0.33x, NBody 0.39x; least on DeltaBlue 0.90x, Json 0.88x, Richards 0.85x); 0.75x of C Lua 5.4 on an Apple M1 Pro; interpreter-only build is 1.8x slower than C Lua 5.5; about 10x faster than go-lua (5.9x C Lua's time); LuaJIT is still 0.18x of C Lua 5.5 (about 3x faster than Apogee's JIT, derived). Embedding suite vs native Go: 5.6x (JIT) vs 7.8x (C Lua 5.5) vs 2.3x (LuaJIT).
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.27.1, CGO_ENABLED=0, -count 6, -ldflags=-funcalign=64, medians; C Lua 5.5.1 and LuaJIT 2.1.1788460057 from Arch Linux packages (their own build flags not stated)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 9900X3D, Linux, pinned to the six cores of one CCD (taskset -c 0-5); also Apple M1 Pro, macOS
tradeoffs: Pure Go with no cgo, so it is not directly usable from C++. Needs Go 1.27.1 or later. The JIT runs only on linux and darwin for arm64 and amd64; elsewhere (Windows included) it interprets at 1.8x C Lua's time. Lua 5.5 semantics but its own binary chunk format; C modules cannot load; C locale only; the collector is Go's with a Lua mark pass for weak tables and finalizers, not incremental.
caveats: Very young project (renamed from luart in September 2026, 0 stars) and the author states a generative AI did much of the engineering. The amd64 and arm64 figures were measured at different commits and the arm64 run compares against C Lua 5.4 (it predates the Lua 5.5 port). Results move up to 10% from one day to the next and C Lua's build flags come from distro packages. LuaJIT remains about 3x faster than Apogee's JIT.
found_via: WebSearch 'Lua implementation faster than PUC-Rio Lua 5.4 interpreter benchmarks github 2026 rewrite embeddable' -> matjam/luart PR #69 (bench: C Lua 5.4 and LuaJIT, and the standard benchmarks); repo has since been renamed to apogee

name: Wangshu (Lua 5.1 VM in Go with tiered JIT)
baseline: gopher-lua (Go implementation of Lua 5.1); no direct PUC Lua or LuaJIT column in the README table
workload: Pure-VM micro benchmarks, three heavy numeric kernels, five Benchmarks Game scripts (fib, binary-trees, spectral-norm, fannkuch, n-body) and Go-to-Lua boundary call and batch-transform workloads, on GitHub Actions runners.
claimed_speedup: P4 method JIT (auto mode) vs gopher-lua on linux/amd64 (Xeon Platinum 8573C): HeavyArith 18.0x, HeavyFloatloop 17.7x, HeavyRecursion 4.8x, fib 9.35x, spectral-norm 15.0x, n-body 14.5x, fannkuch 7.5x, binary-trees 1.9x; the P1 interpreter alone is 3.0-5.5x faster on the three micro kernels but 0.77x on fannkuch and 0.87x on fib; the Go-to-Lua Call boundary is slower than gopher-lua (roughly 0.3-0.6x) and only the zero-allocation CallInto path reaches 0.9-1.5x on the boundary and real-workload rows.
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.27.0 (per go.mod); go test -benchtime=2s -count=3 -cpu=1, median of runs (bench-readme-table workflow, run 29098511106, 2026-07-10); P1 interpreter is the default build, P3/P4 tiers selected with build tags
hardware: GitHub Actions hosted runners: Intel Xeon Platinum 8573C (linux/amd64), Azure Cobalt 100 Neoverse-N2 (linux/arm64), Apple M-series (macos-latest)
stars_or_usage: 8 stars; the README says it runs in production at the author's employer
tradeoffs: Pure Go, no cgo, so not directly usable from C++. Implements Lua 5.1 (no string.dump compatibility, VARARG never compiled by the JIT tiers, limited io). JIT tiers need explicit build tags, and the P5 trace JIT is not implemented. Differential fuzzing against the official Lua 5.1.5 is part of CI.
caveats: The baseline is gopher-lua, a slow Go interpreter, not C Lua or LuaJIT, so it says little about Lua 5.1 proper (the README targets 'LuaJ-luajc or LuaJIT level' but does not show a PUC or LuaJIT column). Numbers come from shared GitHub-hosted VMs (the README warns wall times drift 10-20% between rounds and asks readers to use ratios). The README states the official Lua test suite is only partly covered (about half the lines of most files). The Go-to-Lua call boundary is slower than gopher-lua unless the zero-allocation CallInto path is used.
found_via: github.com/topics/embedded-scripting page (Liam0205/wangshu: 'High-performance pure Go Lua 5.1 virtual machine featuring NaN-boxing, arena GC, and tiered JIT compilation'), then the README performance tables

name: lua-rs (luars, pure Rust Lua 5.5)
workload: 14 script-level microbenchmark files (arithmetic, control flow, locals, functions, closures, multiret, tables, table library, iterators, math, metatables, OOP, coroutines, errors) run by run_benchmarks.ps1 / run_benchmarks.sh, reported as luars throughput divided by native Lua throughput.
claimed_speedup: Windows, Ryzen 7 5800X: arithmetic 111%, locals 132%, table library 118%, coroutines 152%, errors 103% of native Lua throughput, but control flow 87%, functions 92%, closures 80%, multiret 78%, tables 92%, metatables 78%, OOP 92%. macOS (Apple M4, contributor run): all 14 scripts 99% to 301% of native Lua (table library 301%, control flow 143%, arithmetic 136%). The README admits Linux is often 20-40% slower than native Lua on broad coverage.
hardware: Ryzen 7 5800X on Windows; Apple M4 on macOS (reported by a contributor)
tradeoffs: Pure Rust Lua 5.5 runtime with embedding toolkit, derive macros, debugger integration and a WASM target; usable from C++ only through a C boundary the project may expose, not as a drop-in C library. Aims at Lua 5.5 compatibility rather than a different language.
caveats: Mixed result: the project itself says Linux, the most common server platform, is 20-40% slower than native Lua and no Linux snapshot from a physical machine is checked in. Compiler version, Rust flags and how native Lua was built are not stated; the Windows coroutine win is partly an artefact of native Lua's longjmp cost on Windows (the README says so); string microbenchmarks were left out of the Windows chart; macOS numbers come from a third party.
found_via: WebSearch 'Lua implementation faster than PUC-Rio Lua 5.4 interpreter benchmarks github 2026 rewrite embeddable' (result 'lua rs'), then README and docs/benchmarks/windows.md and macos.md

name: Zipp (Rust JavaScript and Python VM)
baseline: QuickJS-NG v0.16.2 (maintained QuickJS fork) for the interpreter; Node.js, Bun and Deno for the JIT builds
workload: Frozen 'real13' set of 13 JavaScript programs and a 5-program micro set run as fresh processes (six counterbalanced repetitions, 10,000-sample bootstrap, exact-output checks) against pinned QuickJS-NG and Boa builds on one Windows x86-64 host; separate canonical captures against Node, Bun and Deno.
claimed_speedup: Interpreter (JIT off) vs QuickJS-NG v0.16.2: real13 geomean 0.6413x of QuickJS-NG's time on v0.0.5 (about 1.56x faster, derived from page data; 12 of 13 point wins) and 0.609x cold-process time on v0.0.6 (13 of 13 wins); micro5 0.8556x. With JITs on, vs Node v24.12.0 / Bun 1.3.14 / Deno 2.6.10: 0.728x of Node's time across 30 workloads (0.614x on the 13 normal rows), launch 7.4 ms vs Node 30.4 ms.
compiler_and_flags: Release build with fat LTO and one codegen unit; Windows PGO build via tools/pgo.sh for the Node/Bun/Deno capture; QuickJS-NG build flags not stated
hardware: Windows 10 build 26200 on 'AMD64 Family 26 Model 68' (AuthenticAMD), read from the raw bench JSON; exact CPU product name not given
tradeoffs: Embeds as a Rust library or runs in the browser as WebAssembly; the browser WASM module was 2.1x slower than QuickJS-NG and 3.6x larger (5.56 MB vs 1.53 MB raw) in the README's own historical capture. Not a drop-in C API. Python frontend is experimental and a GPU lab is bundled, so the crate is large.
caveats: First-party captures, many of them historical: the QuickJS-NG ratios are for v0.0.5 and v0.0.6 and were not repeated on current main; the README reports a later capture (commit 14770703) that is slower against Node and says no headline is claimed for it, and states 'faster than Node on every row' is not yet met (21 of 30 rows). Raw QuickJS-NG artefact files were not located in the bench/ listing. The project is a rapid, largely machine-assisted rewrite with only 6 stars.
found_via: gist 'A list of JavaScript engines, runtimes, interpreters' and github.com/topics/javascript-interpreter and javascript-engine?l=rust pages (f2i-com/zipp.org), then README sections 'Performance, measured honestly' and 'QuickJS-NG and Boa diagnostics'

name: QuickJS-AOT (ivankra/quickjs-aot)
baseline: QuickJS interpreter ('base' column: commit b226856 of ivankra/quickjs, a bellard/quickjs fork)
workload: V8 benchmark suites v7 and v9 (Richards, DeltaBlue, Crypto, RayTrace, EarleyBoyer, RegExp, Splay, NavierStokes, PdfJS, Mandreel, Gameboy, CodeLoad, Box2D, zlib, Typescript), score inversely proportional to runtime, median of 20 runs.
claimed_speedup: qjsc -A (each bytecode function compiled to C by unrolling the interpreter loop) scores 3518 vs 2582 for base QuickJS on the v8-v7 geomean (about 1.36x, derived from page data) and 7784 vs 5425 on v8-v9 (about 1.43x, derived); individual cases up to 2.1x (Crypto 4305 vs 2018, Mandreel 3973 vs 1957). Tail-call dispatch alone reaches 2800 (v8-v7) and 6146 (v8-v9), printed as +25.64% and +26.65% against a reference the page does not name.
compiler_and_flags: Generated C compiled with clang -O2 (bytecode exposed as a static const array for constant folding); clang version and the build flags of the base interpreter are not stated
hardware: Apple Mac M4 running a Debian 13 VM
tradeoffs: Proof-of-concept ahead-of-time compiler: needs a C compiler (clang) at build time and produces a native binary per script, so it only speeds up scripts known at build time; the tail-call dispatch change is separate and easier to adopt (ivankra/quickjs tail branch). Generated C is larger than bytecode.
caveats: First-party numbers with incomplete methodology (compiler version, base build flags, benchmark harness not documented in the README); the percentage columns are relative to an unnamed reference so the table was re-derived against the 'base' column. Gains are workload dependent (RegExp +4%, CodeLoad none) and the author calls the result modest. Github shows no fork link to bellard/quickjs although the README calls it a fork.
found_via: github.com/topics/javascript-engine?l=c page (ivankra/quickjs-aot: 'Ahead-of-time JavaScript compiler: QuickJS with Futamura projection'), then README Results table

name: r8e
baseline: QuickJS (also compared to V8 and Hermes in the same table)
workload: Binary size and runtime memory for a 50 KB application, from the README's 'Key Properties' table.
claimed_speedup: Runtime memory 59 KB vs 136 KB for QuickJS on a 50 KB app (about 2.3x less, derived from page data); binary size about 170 KB vs about 1.5 MB for QuickJS. No speed claim: the README says binary size, memory and security matter more than raw throughput and r8e is a plain bytecode interpreter.
tradeoffs: Subset engine focused on desktop and embedded plugin use with five security layers, built-in UI renderer and font rasteriser; no JIT; C11 with a C API. Not a drop-in for QuickJS (different API).
caveats: Weak evidence: numbers are a first-party table with no method, hardware or build flags; the README mentions a bench/ directory but the root listing shows none; the 1.5 MB QuickJS binary figure looks like a full CLI build (the QuickJS page snippet quotes 367 KiB of x86 code for a hello-world program), so the size ratio is probably overstated. Very young repository (31 commits, 1 star) written with heavy AI assistance (CLAUDE.md present). Included only because the memory claim names QuickJS directly.
found_via: github.com/topics/javascript-engine?l=c page (lightshell-dev/r8e: 'Secure, minimal JavaScript engine in 166KB'), then README 'Key Properties' table

name: LLRT (Low Latency Runtime)
baseline: Node.js 20 on AWS Lambda (not in the list; LLRT itself embeds QuickJS)
workload: Cold-start round-trip time of a DynamoDB put function on AWS Lambda (ARM, 128 MB), LLRT vs Node.js 20, measured as Init Duration plus function duration.
claimed_speedup: README headline: up to over 10x faster startup and up to 2x lower overall cost than other JavaScript runtimes on AWS Lambda; the supporting charts are screenshots (llrt-ddb-put.png vs node20-ddb-put.png) with no numbers in the text.
tradeoffs: Serverless-oriented runtime on QuickJS: no JIT, so peak throughput is far below Node; partial Node API and AWS SDK coverage; the README marks it experimental and for evaluation only.
caveats: First-party vendor claim measured against Node.js 20 on a cold-start metric, not against QuickJS or Lua; numbers are in images, no raw data or flags. Cold-start advantage comes from a small runtime, not from interpreter speed. The benchmarks/ folder holds a V8-suite directory and a streaming fetch script, not the Lambda raw data.
found_via: gist 'A list of JavaScript engines, runtimes, interpreters' (LLRT entry), then README header and 'Benchmark Methodology' section

name: weval (Wasm partial evaluator for interpreters)
baseline: Generic (unspecialised) SpiderMonkey bytecode interpreter running on WebAssembly (StarlingMonkey); not in the list
workload: Ahead-of-time compilation of JavaScript by partially evaluating (wevaling) a WebAssembly build of the SpiderMonkey interpreter with the script's bytecode fixed.
claimed_speedup: README: 'providing 3-5x speedups over the generic interpreter' for wevaled SpiderMonkey builds.
stars_or_usage: 149 stars; used for StarlingMonkey / Wasm JS AOT builds
tradeoffs: Build-time tool, not a scripting engine: the interpreter must be modified with weval intrinsics and scripts must be known at build time; output is a larger Wasm module; engine-specific (SpiderMonkey, PUC-style interpreters need porting work).
caveats: The weval blog post (cfallin.org/blog/2024/08/28/weval/) and paper (arXiv 2411.10559) are linked from the quickjs-aot README but sit on blocked hosts and were not opened; the only figure seen is the README sentence, with no workload, hardware or flags. Baseline is the project's own unspecialised interpreter, not QuickJS, Lua or Duktape, so it only indirectly bears on the category.
found_via: 'Related work' section of the quickjs-aot README (links the cfallin.org weval blog post and the arXiv paper), then the weval README

name: ulua (pure Rust Luau compiler and VM)
baseline: Luau (C++ reference, measured through mlua); Lua 5.4 and LuaJIT 2.1 are in the same chart
workload: Eight compute-heavy cases (recursive Fibonacci, N-Body, Mandelbrot, matrix multiplication, quicksort, string concatenation, binary trees, Spectral Norm) run by an in-memory Rust harness; geometric mean in milliseconds.
claimed_speedup: Interpreter geomean: ulua 40.3 ms vs Lua 5.4 40.4 ms (tie) vs mlua/Luau C++ 52.5 ms (about 1.30x faster than Luau, derived from page data) vs LuaJIT interpreter 36.5 ms. JIT geomean: ulua 23 ms vs mlua/Luau C++ 30.1 ms (about 1.31x, derived) vs LuaJIT 8.4 ms.
hardware: Ubuntu 24.04 aarch64, Neoverse-N2 (4 cores), 16 GB RAM
tradeoffs: Pure Rust (no C toolchain), Luau dialect with a bidirectional type checker, WASM playground, optional AArch64 and x86_64 JIT; not usable from C++ directly. Derived from the pjankiewicz/luaur transliteration of Luau.
caveats: The numbers sit in a chart image (SVG text read directly); the README text only claims parity with C++ Luau in interpretation, and the chart shows Luau C++ via the mlua binding slower than Lua 5.4, which suggests binding or harness overhead in the baseline. Rust and Lua build flags are not stated, and the commit log shows the benchmark configuration being edited on the day of the check. Not faster than Lua 5.4 in interpretation (tie) and 2.7x slower than LuaJIT with JIT on.
found_via: github.com/topics/lua?l=rust page (webc-site/ulua: 'Pure Rust Luau compiler, register VM, and type checker'), then README 'Performance Benchmarks' and the benchmark SVG
